newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU farm ministers set to attack farm reform plans.
newsitem.headline: EU farm ministers set to attack farm reform plans.

text.p: European Union farm ministers, with angry farmers breathing down their necks, are expected to take the offensive on Tuesday against the European Commission's latest plans to cut prices.

EU diplomats said Germany and France were likely to lead the attack during an informal dinner debate after a presentation by Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler of the proposals, designed to prepare for EU expansion eastwards and the next round of world farm trade subsidy cuts.
Published last week, the market-oriented Agenda 2000 blueprint would cut dairy and cereal prices by 10 and 20 percent respectively but only partially compensate farmers for income losses.
"The mood is predictably hostile," said one diplomat, adding that this week's shots would only be the first in a long campaign to dilute the reforms.

But a European Commission spokesman noted that unlike the major 1992 farm reform, which was initially unanimously opposed, there would be qualified support from Britain and Sweden, which both traditionally favour market-oriented reforms.
German Farm Minister Jochen Borchert has already denounced the cuts as unnecessary and unacceptable, saying he will demand major changes.

German farmers' leader Gerd Sonnleitner described the situation as "highly explosive," warning that German farmers, who were already lagging behind workers in other sectors, risked losing one fifth of their incomes.
With elections looming in Germany in 1998, farmers' demands are likely to carry extra weight.

In France, Farm Minister Louis le Pensec has rejected voluntary price cuts ahead of World Trade Organisation (WTO) talks starting at the end of 1999, saying they could force the EU into making further concessions to its trade partners.
Fischler argues that cutting prices to world levels will enable farmers to export without subsidies, escape WTO curbs and increase shipments and earnings.

Price cuts are also deemed necessary to prevent an explosion in EU farm spending and avoid a surge in production surpluses after low cost east European farmers become eligible for EU subsidies after membership.
But French farming unions complain that the reform plans threaten their revenues, jobs and rural development and yield to American pressure to phase out subsidies.
French farmers also fear that a further shift from guaranteed prices and export subsidies towards direct payments would hurt the cereals sector, cost too much and prove unpopular with taxpayers.
Direct payments are estimated to add a net increase of 4.0 billion ecus to farm spending which is expected to climb to 50 billion ecus ($54.9 billion) in 2006, from 43.3 billion in 1999.

Britain, which will chair EU farm reform discussions in the first half of 1998, has welcomed the proposals as "a step in the right direction" but said they should cut costs further, notably in the dairy sector, if enalargement was to be affordable.
But British farmers, who are larger and wealthier than the EU average, oppose plans to limit payments to individual farms.
Fischler wants a fairer distribution of aid, 80 percent of which is grabbed by only 20 percent of farmers, mostly wealthy grain barons in parts of Britain, France and Germany.
